title: Domain, DTO, and record — allocation-aware
hook: A record is a language feature. A DTO is a serialization shape. A domain type is where invariants live. Collapsing the three is how Redis JSON becomes your business model.

sections.heading: Three jobs, three types
sections.prose: A domain `Attempt` has an id that does not change when scores change, a constructor that rejects empty tenant ids, and methods that apply events. Equality is identity, or an explicit value object nested inside. A DTO (`AttemptCacheDto`) exists to round-trip JSON to Redis or an SQS body: public init properties, no behavior, no invariants beyond “serializer succeeded.” A `record` (module 04) gives positional syntax, value equality, and `with`. That is a gift for DTOs and for small value objects (`record struct Money`, `readonly record struct RedisKey`). It is a trap for entities: `attempt with { Score = 0 }` clones without running `ApplyScore`. RabbitMQ messages are DTOs. The consumer maps them into domain commands. Do not share one type across the bus and the aggregate.

snippets.label: Split the cache shape from the entity
snippets.explanation: The record is the Redis JSON contract. ToDomain runs the constructor and ApplyScore. A with-expression on AttemptCacheDto never bypasses that if you do not map blindly.

sections.heading: Allocation: what to copy, what to slice
sections.prose: CSV import (module 17) should parse into primitives and only then construct a DTO or entity. Holding `ReadOnlySpan<char>` inside a class is illegal; you either intern a `string` the domain must own or you keep the row as a stack-local parse. `record struct` DTOs avoid a heap object per row if the fields are small and you do not box them. `record class` DTOs are fine for Redis payloads you already allocate. Collection expressions (C# 12) that build `List<AttemptCacheDto>` from a million rows still allocate a million objects — the syntax did not make it free. Map at the boundary once; do not map DTO → anonymous type → record → entity on every property get.

snippets.label: Parse then allocate once
snippets.explanation: The span dies at the method end. The DTO owns strings it must store. Do not keep a span-based “flyweight entity” on a class field.

sections.heading: Auth tokens and other secrets
sections.prose: An auth token DTO may be a `record` with `string AccessToken` for logging boundaries you must never log. The domain validator (module 16 attributes on the method, not on the record) consumes it and returns a principal. Do not put `Validate()` on the DTO so every serializer instance becomes a security API. Keep behavior on types you version as public API with CI guards (module 16); keep DTOs boring.

interviewTakeaways: Domain types enforce invariants; DTOs serialize; records supply value equality and with-expressions.
Do not with-clone an entity to skip its methods.
Promote span slices to strings only when a heap object must own the data.
commonPitfalls: Using the same record for EF-shaped domain, Redis, and SQS “to save mapping.”
record struct that contains a List — the struct copy is shallow; you thought you were safe.
Parsing CSV into List<string> then into a record — you paid Split and then paid the DTO.

jsTsCorrelations.note: TS interfaces vanish at runtime, so teams often use one type for JSON and behavior. C# types survive in metadata; you can and should keep a class entity distinct from a record DTO.
